content:
# Sirach 41 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** Sirach 41 | **Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Total Disagreements:** 18

---

## Disagreement 1 — 41:1, rendering of "memory" vs. "thought"

**EMET:** "how bitter is the memory of you"
**LOGOS:** "how bitter is the thought of you"
**PNEUMA:** "how bitter the very thought of you is"
**Issue:** Greek mnēmē can mean both "memory" and "thought/reflection." EMET and SOPHIA retain "memory" (more literal); LOGOS and PNEUMA prefer "thought."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "memory" as more literal and preserving the elegiac tone.

---

## Disagreement 2 — 41:1, "has no distractions" vs. "has no worries"

**EMET:** "a man who has no distractions"
**LOGOS:** "the man who has no worries"
**PNEUMA:** "free from worry"
**Issue:** Greek amerimnos means "free from care/worry." EMET chooses "distractions" as more concrete; LOGOS and PNEUMA "worries."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "no distractions" (closer to literal sense of divided attention).

---

## Disagreement 3 — 41:2, "how good" vs. "how welcome"

**EMET:** "how good is your judgment"
**LOGOS:** "how welcome is your sentence"
**PNEUMA:** "how welcome your verdict is"
**Issue:** Greek kalon = "good, fine, welcome." EMET preserves the literal "good"; LOGOS/PNEUMA prefer the idiomatic "welcome."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "welcome" as the more natural English and contextually appropriate rendering.

---

## Disagreement 4 — 41:2, "judgment" vs. "sentence" vs. "verdict" vs. "decree"

**EMET:** "judgment"
**LOGOS:** "sentence"
**PNEUMA:** "verdict"
**Issue:** Greek krisis throughout the chapter for divine/legal decree. Multiple agents disagree on the best legal term.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "decree" in v. 3 (divine), "welcome" + implied verdict in v. 2 to match context.

---

## Disagreement 5 — 41:2, "cantankerous" vs. "stubborn"

**EMET:** "has no patience"
**LOGOS:** "cantankerous and has lost all patience"
**PNEUMA:** "stubborn and has lost all hope"
**Issue:** Greek duskolos means hard to please, difficult, peevish. LOGOS "cantankerous" is most vivid.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "has lost all patience" — combining the sense without the archaic flavor of "cantankerous."

---

## Disagreement 6 — 41:3, "decree" vs. "sentence"

**EMET:** "decree of death"
**LOGOS:** "sentence of death"
**PNEUMA:** "death's decree"
**Issue:** Consistent term for divine disposition. LOGOS "sentence" has legal flavor; EMET "decree" has more authoritative/royal connotation.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "decree" throughout as the standard term.

---

## Disagreement 7 — 41:4, "inquiry" vs. "recrimination" vs. "reckoning"

**EMET:** "there is no inquiry about life in Hades"
**LOGOS:** "there is no recrimination in Hades about the length of one's life"
**PNEUMA:** "no one in Hades is called to account for how long they lived"
**Issue:** Greek ekzētēsis = a searching out, investigation. LOGOS expands to "recrimination" (too strong); PNEUMA paraphrases. EMET "inquiry" is closest.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "reckoning" as a balance between inquiry and accountability.

---

## Disagreement 8 — 41:5, "abominable" vs. "detestable" vs. "contemptible"

**EMET:** "abominable children"
**LOGOS:** "detestable children"
**PNEUMA:** "contemptible children"
**Issue:** Greek bdelukta = abominable, detestable. EMET and LOGOS both capture this; PNEUMA softens to "contemptible."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "abominable" as strongest and most literal.

---

## Disagreement 9 — 41:6, "constant" vs. "perpetual"

**EMET:** "reproach will be constant upon their seed"
**LOGOS:** "perpetual disgrace shall cling to their offspring"
**PNEUMA:** "their descendants will carry their shame forever"
**Issue:** Word choices for the lasting nature of the disgrace. "Perpetual" (LOGOS) and "forever" (PNEUMA) are stronger than "constant" (EMET).
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "perpetual reproach" — most literal and appropriately solemn.

---

## Disagreement 10 — 41:11, "mourning" vs. "grief"

**EMET:** "The mourning of men is about their body"
**LOGOS:** "The mourning of men is over their bodies"
**PNEUMA:** "People mourn over a dead body"
**Issue:** Minor structural difference. All convey the same meaning. PNEUMA loses the contrast with the evil name.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows LOGOS/EMET closely: "The mourning of men is over their bodies."

---

## Disagreement 11 — 41:11, "wiped out" vs. "blotted out"

**EMET:** "wiped out"
**LOGOS:** "blotted out"
**PNEUMA:** "wiped out completely"
**Issue:** Greek exaleiphthēsetai = to blot out, erase. "Blotted out" has more scriptural resonance (cf. Ps. 69:28).
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "blotted out."

---

## Disagreement 12 — 41:12, "treasuries" vs. "hoards"

**EMET:** "thousand great treasuries of gold"
**LOGOS:** "thousands of great hoards of gold"
**PNEUMA:** "any treasure trove of gold"
**Issue:** Greek thēsaurōn = treasuries, storehouses. "Treasuries" (EMET) is most literal; "hoards" (LOGOS) is more vivid; PNEUMA loses the "thousand" intensifier.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET: "a thousand great treasuries of gold."

---

## Disagreement 13 — 41:14, "take hold of" vs. "keep" vs. "live"

**EMET:** "take hold of instruction in peace"
**LOGOS:** "keep instruction in peace"
**PNEUMA:** "live your instruction in peace"
**Issue:** Greek kratēsate = seize, take hold of, keep. EMET is most literal; LOGOS captures the sense of maintenance; PNEUMA is too interpretive.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "keep instruction in peace" as most natural English.

---

## Disagreement 14 — 41:15, word order and framing

**EMET:** "Better is the person who conceals his folly than the man who conceals his wisdom"
**LOGOS:** "Better is the person who hides his folly than the one who hides his wisdom"
**PNEUMA:** "Better someone who hides their foolishness than someone who hides their wisdom"
**Issue:** Minor variations only. PNEUMA uses gender-neutral "their" anachronistically. "Folly" vs. "foolishness" — Greek aphrosunēn = lack of wisdom.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS: "Better is the person who conceals his folly than one who conceals his wisdom."

---

## Disagreement 15 — 41:16, "partiality" vs. same

**EMET:** "show partiality in every matter"
**LOGOS:** "show partiality in every matter"
**PNEUMA:** "the same standard"
**Issue:** Greek prosōpolēmpsia = partiality, favoritism. PNEUMA paraphrases. EMET/LOGOS agree.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 16 — 41:20, "leaning/reclining on your elbow"

**EMET:** "leaning upon your elbow at a meal"
**LOGOS:** "resting on your elbow at table"
**PNEUMA:** "lounging at table on your elbow"
**Issue:** Greek en anaklisei agoū = at the inclining of the elbow — reclining at Hellenistic dinner. PNEUMA's "lounging" is slightly pejorative.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "reclining on your elbow at table" (LOGOS) as most natural.

---

## Disagreement 17 — 41:21, "selfishness in receiving and giving" vs. "scorning when someone gives and takes away"

**EMET:** "of scorning when someone gives and takes away"
**LOGOS:** "of selfishness in receiving and giving"
**PNEUMA:** "of grabbing without giving"
**Issue:** Greek text is ambiguous; different agents read the syntax differently. EMET follows a more literal Greek reading; LOGOS interprets as selfishness in transactions.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts LOGOS's reading: "of selfishness in giving and receiving" — clearer English.

---

## Disagreement 18 — 41:27, "truly ashamed" vs. "truly modest"

**EMET:** "you will be truly ashamed"
**LOGOS:** "you will be truly modest"
**PNEUMA:** "you will show real modesty"
**Issue:** Greek aischunthēsē = to be ashamed/modest. In context this is positive — the constructive shame that produces good character. "Modest" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) captures the positive valence better than "ashamed."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "truly modest."

---

*Total disagreements logged: 18*
